title: BFS / DFS
summary: Two ways to systematically visit every reachable node in a graph or grid — level by level, or all the way down one path first.
explanation: Breadth-first search (BFS) and depth-first search (DFS) both visit every node reachable from a starting point exactly once, using a 'visited' set to avoid repeats — but they explore in a different order, which makes them suited to different questions.

BFS uses a queue (FIFO). It visits the start node, then all of its direct neighbors, then all of their unvisited neighbors, and so on — expanding outward in layers. Because it explores in layers, the first time BFS reaches a node is guaranteed to be via a shortest path (in terms of number of edges), which is why BFS is the go-to for shortest-path and 'minimum steps' problems on unweighted graphs.

DFS uses a stack (either explicitly, or implicitly via recursion). It visits the start node, then dives into one neighbor, then one of that neighbor's neighbors, and keeps going deeper until it hits a dead end — then backtracks and tries the next unexplored branch. DFS is the natural fit for 'does a path exist', 'find all connected components', cycle detection, and problems where you need to explore a full path before deciding it's good (like backtracking).
whenToUse: BFS: you need the shortest path or minimum number of steps in an unweighted graph or grid.
BFS: you need to process nodes level-by-level (e.g. level-order tree traversal).
DFS: you need to explore every path, detect cycles, or find connected components.
DFS: the recursive/backtracking structure of the problem naturally matches 'go deep, then undo and try another branch'.
